sources.news_title: Judge orders the Trump administration to cancel taxpayer-funded promotional TV ads - WXXV News 25
sources.text:
Judge orders the Trump administration to cancel taxpayer-funded promotional TV ads
President Donald Trump must cancel any remaining television commercials paid for with millions of dollars in taxpayer money to promote his political message, a federal judge ordered Sunday night, even as the administration said the ad campaign was coming to an end.
U.S. District Judge Jennifer L. Rochon in New York sided with a coalition, including the nonpartisan watchdog Common Cause, that challenged the ads as an illegal misuse of funds. She told the administration to cancel any remaining ads, including any set to air Sunday night, in granting a temporary restraining order.
“Defendants shall not enter into, renew, or expand any agreement authorizing the development, creation, dissemination, placement, or airing of the challenged advertisements” during the two-week duration of her order, the judge said.
Asked for comment, the White House referred to an Oct. 5 social media post from Trump in which he defended the taxpayer-funded ads as “rather standard” but, amid backlash, said he would pay for them from his political fundraising. In a court filing late Saturday, the Justice Department argued that the temporary restraining order was unnecessary because “the alleged offending conduct will end tomorrow.”
The Department of Homeland Security tapped $20 million in taxpayer money for the ads. Legal experts have suggested that violated a federal statute against congressionally appropriated money being used for “publicity or propaganda” and potentially other laws.
“We are pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda,” the plaintiffs said in a statement issued by Democracy Forward, the nonprofit legal organization that represents them. “There is no legal justification — and no precedent — for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda.”
In a court declaration Saturday, senior DHS official Holly Mehringer wrote that the money came from funds appropriated by Congress that are “available for, among other things, ‘commemorating efforts and events related to border security.’”
The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements akin to what past administrations have done to promote various policies. But the recent ads differ from many past public service announcements because they aren’t aimed at helping members of the public benefit from specific government programs.
The ads, which began airing in late September, glorify Trump and echo his political messaging going into the midterms. One features a clip of Trump talking about the threat of communism and another is a replay of an ad from his last presidential campaign. The fifth ad in the campaign began airing Tuesday, focusing on the Trump administration’s capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro.
The use of public funds to pay for the ads drew heavy criticism — including from some in the GOP.
“It shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters.
The Democratic National Committee has separately sued the Republican administration over the ads.
Amid the backlash, Trump said he would start paying for the ads with a campaign account. A White House official said there were no immediate plans to reimburse the government for money already spent.

EXCLUSIVE: Trump's $20Million Taxpayer-Funded Ad Blitz Shut Down by Federal Judge — as White House Ordered to Pull Commercials
Oct. 12 2026, Published 3:23 p.m. ET
President Donald Trump's $20million taxpayer-funded television advertising campaign has been brought to an abrupt halt after a federal judge ordered his administration to pull a series of commercials off the air amid a legal battle over government spending, RadarOnline.com can exclusively reveal.
According to court documents obtained by Radar, U.S. District Judge Jennifer L. Rochon issued a temporary restraining order on October 11, blocking the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) from using federal funds to produce, distribute or broadcast the challenged advertisements.
Judge Halts $20Million Ad Blitz
The ruling comes amid a lawsuit accusing the Trump administration of improperly using taxpayer money to promote the president ahead of the November 2026 midterm elections.
"Defendants shall cancel or cause to be cancelled any slot, placement, reservation, or arrangement for the airing or dissemination of the challenged advertisements," Rochon ordered.
The court also suspended a September 20 advertising contract involving Customs and Border Protection and LMD Agency, covering five disputed commercials.
Court Sides With Challengers
The restrictions covered commercials scheduled to air on October 11 and barred federal officials from expanding existing advertising arrangements or entering new ones.
The lawsuit was brought by Common Cause, Robert Hunter, Service Employees International Union Local 32BJ, and Empire State 32BJ SEIU PAC.
The plaintiffs allege that the administration exceeded congressional spending authorizations and violated federal restrictions concerning government publicity and propaganda.
In granting emergency relief, Rochon determined that the plaintiffs demonstrated they were likely to succeed on the merits of their claims.
Judge Cites 'Irreparable Harm'
The judge also found the plaintiffs would suffer irreparable harm without an injunction and that granting relief served the public interest.
The ruling follows an October 9 conference during which government attorneys did not provide relevant information addressing the request for immediate relief, according to the order.
The court subsequently allowed expedited briefing before issuing its decision.
The court's intervention followed an emergency request by the plaintiffs, who argued that allowing the advertisements to continue would cause harm that could not be adequately remedied later.
White House Faces Compliance Deadline
The administration must also submit a status report within 24 hours confirming compliance with the restrictions. The temporary restraining order took effect at 6:45 p.m. on October 11 and will remain in place for 14 days unless extended.
Although the judge indicated that a fuller written opinion would follow, the ruling does not represent a final determination that the advertising expenditures were unlawful.
The court also canceled a previously scheduled October 13 conference, which will be rescheduled to address the litigation's next steps.
The temporary order leaves the broader legal dispute unresolved, with the court still weighing whether the administration exceeded its spending authority and violated federal restrictions on government-funded publicity.

Judge Orders Trump Administration To Pull Taxpayer-Funded Ads Praising President
A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to stop using taxpayer-funded ads that portray President Donald Trump favorably right before the midterms.
According to NBC News, the lawsuit was filed by the watchdog group “Common Cause; Robert Hunter, a Democratic candidate for a seat in the Alabama state House, and a labor union in New York and its political action committee.”
The suit was one of many filed—including one by the Democratic National Committee—to get the government-funded ads that show the president in the most favorable light ever off the air.
“Plaintiffs have demonstrated that they are likely to succeed on the merits, will suffer irreparable harm in the absence of an injunction, the balance of the equities tips in their favor, and an injunction serves the public interest,” U.S. District Judge Jennifer Rochon of the Southern District of New York wrote, NBC News reports.
In a court filing Saturday, the administration claimed the Department of Homeland Security used a vendor to place ad buys through Sunday and told the vendor not to purchase ads after Sunday.
The Judge ordered the Trump administration “cancel or cause to be cancelled” any ads, including those scheduled to run Sunday night, off the air.
The judge also added that the administration was no longer allowed to use funds allocated for the DHS to “develop, create, disseminate, place, distribute, publish, or air the challenged advertisements.”
Trump said last week that MAGA Inc. would help fund the ads going forward.
“We are pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda,” the plaintiffs said in a statement to NBC News. “There is no legal justification — and no precedent — for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda.”
Common Cause President and CEO Virginia Kase Solomón said that despite the ruling and the fact that the Trump administration knows better, “our fight continues.”
“We won’t stop until this administration is held fully accountable, and no president from any party can waste and abuse taxpayer funds for propaganda ever again,” Solomón said.
The ads were so egregious that one was nearly identical to a 2024 Trump campaign ad that had critics in an uproar because, at the very end, it noted that the U.S. Government paid for it.

sources.news_title: BREAKING: Biden-Appointed Judge Blocks DHS Border Ads Featuring Trump — Just 24 Hours Before Election
sources.text:
A federal judge appointed by former President Joe Biden issued an injunction Sunday evening ordering the Department of Homeland Security to halt a taxpayer-funded television advertising campaign featuring President Donald Trump — even though the administration had already told the court the ads were scheduled to end that same day.
U.S.
The lawsuit was filed by the watchdog group Common Cause, Robert Hunter, a Democratic candidate for a seat in the Alabama state House, and a labor union in New York and its political action committee, NBC News reported. It was one of several similar complaints — including one from the Democratic National Committee — filed to get the ads off the air, according to the same outlet.
The administration had said in a court filing Saturday that DHS, through a vendor, had placed ad buys through Sunday and had told the vendor not to purchase ads beyond that day, per NBC News. Rochon nonetheless rejected the argument that the case was moot.
The ads have been criticized as government propaganda aimed at influencing the outcome of the midterm election, according to the Guardian. The total advertising purchase was reported at $20 million.
"Plaintiffs have demonstrated that they are likely to succeed on the merits, will suffer irreparable harm in the absence of an injunction, the balance of the equities tips in their favor, and an injunction serves the public interest," Rochon wrote, according to NBC News.
The injunction arrives as the nation barrels toward Election Day, with early voting already underway in dozens of states. It is not yet known whether the administration will appeal the ruling or how quickly the vendor will comply with the cancellation order.
Critics of the ruling point out that federal courts are now being used to police political speech funded through the executive branch — a novel use of judicial power at a moment when the administration says its border messaging serves a legitimate public safety function. Supporters of the injunction argue that using federal tax dollars to promote a sitting president's image crosses a line that even the administration seemed to recognize when it let the ad buys lapse.
The case is one of several fronts where Democratic-aligned groups are testing the limits of executive communications. The DNC's separate complaint remains pending, according to NBC News, and could produce additional rulings in the days ahead. It remains unclear how much money has already been spent on the ad campaign or whether any additional media buys were placed in other markets outside the New York court's reach.
Our Take
Patriots, let's call this what it is.
A judge hand-picked by the Biden administration just told the Department of Homeland Security — the agency tasked with keeping America's borders secure — that it cannot run ads telling the American people what it is doing. Not because the ads were false. Not because they endangered anyone. But because they featured President Trump.
Think about the timing. The administration told the court the ads were already wrapping up Sunday. That wasn't good enough. The judge still issued an emergency order to kill ads that were about to stop running on their own. This wasn't about stopping alleged election interference. This was about making a statement — and making it before Election Day.
Where were these same watchdog groups when the Biden regime used federal agencies to coordinate censorship with Big Tech? Where was Common Cause when the FBI was labeling parents as domestic terrorists for speaking at school board meetings? The silence was deafening.
This is the two-tier justice system in broad daylight. Conservative speech gets enjoined. Left-wing activism gets funded. And unelected judges in Manhattan get to decide what the American people are allowed to see in the final days of an election.
The question now is simple: Will the administration fight this, or will it let a single district judge in New York dictate what the federal government can say to the public? Americans deserve to know where their government stands — and whether the people they elected still have the power to speak.
Stay tuned. This one is not over.

sources.news_title: Judge Halts Taxpayer-Funded Trump Ads Ahead of Midterms
sources.text:
A federal judge in New York ordered the Trump administration Sunday night to immediately stop airing government-funded television ads featuring President Donald Trump that critics say were designed to influence November’s midterm elections.
Judge Jennifer Rochon’s temporary restraining order also bars the Department of Homeland Security from spending any more money from the $20 million allocated for the campaign. About $19 million has already been spent.
Congress appropriated the money for immigration enforcement. The ads, which have aired for weeks, carry the caption “Paid for by the U.S. Government.”
The order lasts 14 days unless extended. It requires the administration to cancel scheduled broadcasts and prohibits new agreements or expansions of existing contracts for the ads.
The ruling came after government attorneys told the court the ads would stop airing after Sunday. A coalition challenging the campaign argued that a court order was still necessary because broadcasts remained scheduled that evening, potentially reaching millions of viewers.
Rochon agreed that the administration’s promised cutoff did not eliminate the need for action. She also rejected the Justice Department’s argument that the coalition lacked legal standing to sue.
The judge found that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed in their lawsuit, would suffer irreparable harm without an order and that blocking the ads served the public interest. She said a fuller opinion explaining her decision would follow.
The coalition, which includes Common Cause and Service Employees International Union Local 32BJ, filed its lawsuit Oct. 7. The Democratic National Committee filed a separate challenge that day.
Democrats have criticized the ads as an effort to help Republicans in the November elections, which will determine control of Congress.
One ad, titled “The Country He Loves,” mixes images of Trump with statements promoting his administration’s accomplishments, including tax cuts, manufacturing and support for police. It repeatedly flashes a message declaring that America will never be a communist country.
Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., questioned the campaign in a Sept. 24 letter to White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, saying it appeared to violate federal restrictions on using taxpayer money for political propaganda.
Trump said Oct. 5 that he or his super PAC, MAGA Inc., would pay for future ads. The White House later said he would not reimburse the government for those already aired.
The coalition welcomed the ruling, saying taxpayer dollars should not finance political messaging intended to influence elections.
The Manhattan U.S. Attorney’s Office declined to comment. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

sources.news_title: 'Purely partisan': Trump in judge's crosshairs after shutting down 'propaganda' ads
sources.text:
A federal judge pointed to President Donald Trump's personal involvement in taxpayer-funded TV ads that "likely" violated the law by airing ahead of the midterms, noting his administration did not contest that the ads were “purely partisan.”
After issuing a restraining order to shut down the ads on Sunday, U.S. District Judge Jennifer L. Rochon explained her reasoning in an opinion filed Monday in Manhattan federal court.
The government paid for the ads with Department of Homeland Security money that Congress set aside for border security, even though the ads praise the president and cast his perceived adversaries in sharply negative terms, Rochon wrote.
Government lawyers did not try to defend the ads as legal, Rochon noted. In a court filing Saturday, they argued instead that the case was moot, meaning no longer a live dispute, because the ad buys would end Sunday. They also argued the plaintiffs had no legal right to sue.
A provision of federal spending law known as Section 718 bars agencies from using taxpayer money “for publicity or propaganda purposes” that Congress has not approved, Rochon explained.
“Defendants do not contest that the at-issue advertisements are purely partisan and unconnected to DHS’s official functions,” Rochon wrote. “Thus, the Court finds that Moving Plaintiffs are likely to succeed in showing that the advertisements are impermissible ‘publicity or propaganda’ under Section 718.”
“Indeed, the ‘Final Battle’ advertisement is almost identical to one used during President Trump’s 2024 campaign, other than the fact that its funding disclaimer now identifies the United States government rather than his presidential campaign,” the judge wrote.
In that ad, Trump vows to “demolish the deep state,” “cast out the communists, Marxists, and fascists” and “rout the fake news media,” according to the opinion.
“This advertisement provides no information about DHS’s official functions,” Rochon added.
The money came from a $6.168 billion border security fund Congress approved in July 2025, according to the opinion. One listed use was “[c]ommemorating efforts and events related to border security,” which a House report described with examples such as line-of-duty death memorials, agency anniversaries and commendation ceremonies.
The White House budget office approved a request to shift an extra $20 million into that category within two hours on Sept. 19, the opinion said. The ads began airing four days later.
Rochon also found the plaintiffs have the right to sue. She agreed, citing an earlier ruling, that the ads “fundamentally alter the environment” for Robert Hunter, the Democratic nominee for Alabama House District 28 and a democratic socialist, by attacking socialism under a government label.
“Indeed, this appears to be the advertising campaign’s intended goal,” Rochon wrote.
She noted that the government did not dispute that "President Trump, along with Wiles and others, met with Republican political strategists to discuss the upcoming elections and the use of funds from MAGA Inc., a political action committee, to support Republican candidates in the midterm elections" on Aug. 7.
“Thus, Plaintiffs are likely to succeed in showing that the challenged advertisements were disseminated to support Republican candidates and impact the midterm elections,” Rochon wrote.
Hunter said in a court declaration that his campaign has spent $1,812 on advertising and that the government ads ran far more widely in his district.
Absentee and early voting are already underway in states including Alabama and New York, she noted.
Rochon wrote that the Constitution’s spending clause exists to ensure public money is spent according to Congress’s judgments about the common good, so any alleged violation is “in contravention of that common good and against the public interest.”

sources.news_title: Trump ordered to stop taxpayer-funded ads promoting himself
sources.text:
Donald Trump has been ordered by a federal judge to cancel all taxpayer-funded television ads that were promoting himself.
The US president received backlash from both Democrats and Republicans over the issue, which arrived just weeks ahead of the highly-contested upcoming midterm elections.
It has been reported in the States that the Trump administration has paid for ads promoting the 80-year-old with $20 million of Department of Homeland Security funds.
A temporary restraining order has since been issued by US District Judge Jennifer Rochon, who has stopped the administration from creating or airing such ads for 14 days.
In the court order, Rochon stated: ‘Defendants shall not enter into, renew, or expand any agreement authorizing the development, creation, dissemination, placement, or airing of the challenged advertisements.’
The order added that plaintiffs alleged the ads ‘exceed the purposes authorised by Congress and violate restrictions on publicity and propaganda’.
In a statement issued by Democracy Forward, the plaintiffs said: ‘We are pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda.
‘There is no legal justification – and no precedent – for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda.’
While Trump is not on the midterm elections ballot, he has been campaigning for Republican candidates amid rising Democratic support.
The White House has defended the taxpayer-funded ads, claiming that they were public service announcements.
The first ad was aired in late September, featuring Trump saying: ‘America will never be a communist country.’
Another one showed Trump warning of a ‘final battle’ over black-and-white footage of him walking down a hallway.
The second ad included an onscreen message that read: ‘Paid for by the US government.’
Democratic Senator John Hickenlooper slammed the ads as ‘illegal’ and ‘propaganda’, with some senior Republicans also expressing concern over them.
Last week on Truth Social, Trump wrote that he and his political campaign would pay for the ads promoting himself.

sources.news_title: Trump Says He’ll Pay for Political Ads, but Taxpayers Already Footed Millions as Judge Orders Halt
sources.text:
By Lucretia Hughes Klucken
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump’s promise to personally finance controversial television advertisements promoting his administration has raised a significant question following a federal judge’s order halting the campaign: If Trump says he is paying for the ads himself, why were millions of taxpayer dollars used to finance them in the first place?
U.S. District Judge Jennifer L. Rochon, a Biden appointee serving in the Southern District of New York, issued a temporary restraining order Sunday, October 11, directing the Trump administration to cancel remaining government-funded television advertisements. The order followed a lawsuit challenging whether federal agencies improperly spent taxpayer money on political messaging ahead of November’s midterm elections.
At the center of the controversy is a $20 million advertising contract awarded by the Department of Homeland Security to LMD Agency for a national media campaign that began airing in September.
According to federal contracting records and court filings, the advertisements were initially financed through congressional appropriations administered by DHS. The funding was connected to border security initiatives and commemorative activities, rather than private campaign donations.
Media tracking firm AdImpact reported that more than $12 million had already been spent airing the advertisements when legal challenges were filed earlier this month.
Trump defended the campaign in an October 5 Truth Social post, describing the advertisements as positive promotion of the United States and arguing that government-funded messaging about presidential policies was not unusual.
However, following criticism from Democrats and Republicans, Trump announced that future advertisements would be financed through his political fundraising, including money associated with MAGA Inc., a super PAC supporting his political agenda.
That announcement did not establish that Trump had personally reimbursed the federal government for advertisements already purchased or broadcast.
A White House official subsequently indicated that there were no immediate plans to reimburse taxpayers for the previously incurred expenses.
The distinction is significant. Paying for future advertisements through private political contributions does not erase federal expenditures already made. Nor does a presidential pledge to assume future advertising costs automatically transfer previous government obligations to a private account.
The White House has maintained that the advertisements were legitimate public service announcements intended to inform Americans about administration policies. Officials argued that previous presidential administrations have also used federal funds to communicate government initiatives.
Critics contend that the advertisements went beyond ordinary government communications by prominently featuring Trump, repeating campaign-style messages and promoting his political leadership shortly before the midterm elections.
One advertisement closely resembled material used during Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign. Another featured the president discussing communism, while additional spots highlighted administration accomplishments.
The legal dispute centers on federal restrictions against using congressionally appropriated funds for unauthorized publicity or propaganda.
Federal agencies generally may use public funds to explain government programs, policies and services. However, federal appropriations law restricts the use of those funds for certain partisan or unauthorized promotional activities.
The Democratic National Committee filed one lawsuit challenging the advertisements. A separate coalition, including the government watchdog organization Common Cause, also sought judicial intervention.
Rochon sided with the coalition in issuing a two-week temporary restraining order, preventing the administration from continuing or expanding agreements involving the challenged advertisements.
The ruling does not constitute a final judgment that the administration violated federal law. Instead, the judge determined that the plaintiffs had demonstrated sufficient grounds for temporary judicial relief while the litigation continues.
The Justice Department argued that court intervention was unnecessary because the government-funded advertising campaign was already scheduled to conclude.
Republican lawmakers also questioned the original financing arrangement.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., publicly opposed using taxpayer dollars for the advertisements. Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., similarly questioned whether government officials should use public money for promotional advertisements centered on themselves.
Their objections demonstrate that concerns about federal spending in this case have extended beyond partisan disagreements over the president.
The controversy also raises broader questions about presidential authority, congressional oversight and the distinction between official government communications and political advertising.
The administration’s position is that the advertisements promoted government policies. The plaintiffs argue that public funds were diverted toward messaging intended to benefit the president and his political allies.
For taxpayers, the financial question remains unresolved.
The available evidence establishes that the federal government originally funded the advertising campaign through a $20 million DHS contract. Trump subsequently pledged to finance future advertisements using private political funds, but the administration has not confirmed reimbursement of the millions already spent.
The court’s order temporarily stops the challenged government-funded advertisements, but it does not itself return money to the Treasury.
A hearing is scheduled for October 13 to determine the next steps in the litigation.
Until the administration provides documentation establishing which expenses were transferred to private funding and whether previously spent taxpayer dollars will be reimbursed, Trump’s promise to pay does not change the documented source of the original advertising expenditures.
The fundamental issue is not whether a president can promote his policies. It is whether Congress authorized taxpayer money to be spent on these particular advertisements and whether the federal government or private political donors ultimately bear the cost.

sources.news_title: Federal Judge Throws a Wrench Into Trump's $20 Million Ad Blitz Ahead of Midterms
sources.text:
A federal judge in New York has temporarily halted a $20 million government-funded advertising campaign featuring President Donald Trump ahead of the November midterm elections, finding that the plaintiffs challenging the expenditure are likely to prevail on their claims that the funding ran afoul of federal appropriations laws.
U.S. District Judge Jennifer Rochon, a Biden appointee, issued a temporary restraining order Sunday evening, directing the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to stop funding the advertisements and cancel scheduled broadcasts. She followed up Monday with a 40-page opinion explaining her reasoning.
The lawsuit, brought by Common Cause, an Alabama Democratic legislative candidate, and a labor union and its political action committee, challenges the administration's use of funds appropriated for border-security purposes to pay for television advertisements highlighting Trump's accomplishments and criticizing political ideologies and opponents.
The administration opposed the request for emergency relief, arguing that the plaintiffs lacked standing to sue and that the dispute was effectively moot because DHS had already decided to stop purchasing the advertisements. It did not separately contest the plaintiffs' arguments regarding the applicable spending restrictions at this preliminary stage. But Rochon rejected the jurisdictional arguments.
How the Advertising Campaign Was Funded
According to the court's opinion, Customs and Border Protection (CBP) requested an additional $20 million allocation for commemorating border-security efforts on September 19. The Office of Management and Budget approved the request approximately 95 minutes later. The following day, CBP issued a $20 million purchase order to LMD Agency for a national media campaign, with the advertisements beginning to air September 23.
The campaign included five advertisements identified in the lawsuit, including one titled "Final Battle," which closely resembled an advertisement from Trump's 2024 presidential campaign. The newer version omitted the appeal to vote for Trump and identified the U.S. government as its sponsor.
By October 8, the advertisements had aired more than 16,000 times, generating an estimated 1.56 billion impressions at an estimated cost of $15.4 million, according to figures submitted by the plaintiffs.
The funding came from a congressional appropriation covering several border-security activities, including commemorating border-security efforts and events. Rochon examined the statutory language and legislative history, concluding that Congress intended the commemorative category to cover matters such as memorials, agency anniversaries, and recognition ceremonies rather than the advertising campaign at issue.
Why the Judge Intervened
Rochon found that the plaintiffs had demonstrated a substantial likelihood of succeeding on claims involving two federal spending restrictions. The first, known as the Purpose Statute, generally requires federal agencies to spend appropriated funds for the purposes Congress authorized. The second restricts using federal appropriations for unauthorized publicity or propaganda, including materials designed to benefit a political party or candidate.
The judge also determined that the plaintiffs had standing to bring the challenge because the advertisements potentially disadvantaged candidates and political organizations competing against the messages they conveyed.
President Trump announced on October 5 that he would begin paying for the advertisements himself and using funds raised through MAGA Inc. The administration subsequently informed the court that DHS-funded media purchases would end October 11. However, Rochon found that the existing agreement, outstanding payments, and possibility of additional spending meant the administration's representations did not eliminate the need for temporary relief.
Her order stays the $20 million purchase agreement and the corresponding funding allocation, prevents further DHS expenditures on the challenged advertisements, and requires cancellation of existing placements. It also directs the advertising contractor to stop running the spots. The order remains effective for 14 days, subject to extension.
Bear in mind: The ruling is preliminary, not a final determination that the administration violated federal law. Nor does it generally prohibit Trump or political organizations from financing advertisements using private funds.
For now, the dispute turns on a narrower question: whether the funding Congress authorized for border-security-related activities could be used for this particular advertising campaign. Rochon concluded that the plaintiffs are likely to prevail on their argument that it could not.

MANHATTAN (CN) — President Donald Trump’s collection of taxpayer-funded TV advertisements, airing for the past two weeks ahead of the midterm election cycle, was likely a violation of the Administrative Procedure Act, a federal judge ruled Monday.
U.S. District Judge Jennifer Rochon, a Joe Biden appointee in the Southern District of New York, issued a brief order Sunday night directing the government to immediately cease use of the controversial advertisements. Monday morning, she explained her decision in a 40-page order, in which she found the Trump administration was using taxpayer funds appropriated for border security for what could be considered “publicity or propaganda purposes.”
“Indeed, the ‘Final Battle’ advertisement is almost identical to one used during President Trump’s 2024 campaign, other than the fact that its funding disclaimer now identifies the United States government rather than his presidential campaign,” she noted.
“It depicts President Trump walking down a hallway while delivering a series of statements about his political adversaries,” Rochon wrote of the commercial. “Among other things, he promises to ‘demolish the deep state,’ ‘drive out the globalists,’ ‘cast out the communists, Marxists and fascists,’ ‘throw off the sick political class that hates our country,’ and ‘rout the fake news media.’”
The Trump administration has likened the commercials to public service announcements rather than political advertisements.
But despite being backed by funding from the Department of Homeland Security, Rochon wrote, “This advertisement provides no information about DHS’s official functions.”
The ruling came in response to a lawsuit brought last week by watchdog group Common Cause, two labor unions and a Democratic candidate for Alabama’s state House of Representatives, who claimed the “overtly political” ads were a result of $20 million of unlawful budget maneuvering by DHS.
“Congress has made clear for the last 75 years that, absent explicit congressional approval, the executive is forbidden to spend taxpayer funds on personal publicity and political propaganda,” the groups argue in their complaint. “And it’s hard to imagine government ads that flout those prohibitions more than Trump’s taxpayer-funded ads.”
When reached for comment on Rochon’s ruling Monday, the White House referred to a Truth Social post from Trump on Oct. 5, in which he referred to the ads as “positive promotion for our great U.S.A.”
DHS didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
The plaintiffs said in a statement they were “pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda.”
“There is no legal justification — and no precedent — for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda,” they said.
Even prior to Monday’s ruling, the Trump administration had agreed to swap the funding for these commercials from taxpayers to right-wing PACs. DHS informed Rochon over the weekend there were “no plans” to continue running the commercials on the agency’s dime.
That was the crux of the administration’s argument against the lawsuit — not that the ads were a lawful use of taxpayer funds, but that the case was moot since the government agreed not to run them anymore.
“Defendants did not contest that the placements for the challenged advertisements were paid for by taxpayer appropriated funds for border security, technology and screening and did not dispute plaintiffs’ contention that use of those funds violated the Purpose Act and the Appropriations Act,” Rochon wrote in her order.
The government is facing another lawsuit over the ads in federal court in Washington, D.C., where the Democratic National Committee sued to stop what it claims is a flailing, unlawful bid to save Republicans’ poor poll numbers ahead of the midterms.
“The Trump administration’s illegal use of taxpayer dollars for campaign-style advertisements deprives the DNC of a fair electoral process by adding public funds to the resources available to support Republican candidates,” the committee writes in its complaint. “The use of public funds also places the DNC and Democratic candidates at an electoral disadvantage, even though the publicly funded propaganda advertisements are deeply unpopular with American voters, by preserving funds held by campaign committees and PACs — including MAGA Inc. — for other political expenditures.”
The judge has yet to rule in that case.

They end with a disclaimer saying they were paid for by the US government.

The Department of Homeland Security tapped $20 million (€17.8 million) taxpayer funds to run the ads in question.

President Trump must cancel any remaining television commercials paid for with millions of dollars in taxpayer money to promote his political message, a federal judge ordered Sunday night, even as the administration said the ad campaign was coming to an end.
U.S. District Judge Jennifer L. Rochon in New York sided with a coalition, including the nonpartisan watchdog Common Cause, which challenged the ads as an illegal misuse of funds. She ordered the administration to cancel any remaining ads, including any set to air Sunday night, in granting a temporary restraining order.
"Defendants shall not enter into, renew, or expand any agreement authorizing the development, creation, dissemination, placement, or airing of the challenged advertisements" during the two-week duration of her order, the judge said.
The order was in effect as of 6:45 p.m. ET on Sunday.
The spending on cable and broadcast for the five Trump ads that disclose on screen that they were "paid for by the U.S. Government" now exceeds $20 million, according to political ad tracker AdImpact. That's the amount the Department of Homeland Security had allocated for a "National Media Campaign," awarding a contract for the ads to Maryland-based LMD Agency on Sept. 20. A day earlier, the White House Office of Management and Budget had granted DHS's Customs and Border Protection $20 million for "OBBB Commemorative Events," according to a nongovernment database. The source of the funds was first reported by The Washington Sun.
By Monday morning, AdImpact showed U.S. government spending on the five ads had reached $21,705,138. (Because the ads were classified by the White House as PSAs, AdImpact may not reflect the exact total amount spent.)
Here are the five ads listed in AdImpact and the amount spent, as of Monday:
- Maduro ($3.1 million): Featuring Mr. Trump, Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Dan Caine, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio talk about the operation to capture and remove Nicolás Maduro from power in Venezuela.
- Final Battle ($13 million): A refurbished version of a Trump 2024 campaign video shows Mr. Trump walking down the hallway as part of a Trump campaign speech plays. He can be heard vowing "once and for all" to "demolish the deep state," "expel the warmongers from our government," "throw off the sick political class that hates our country" and "rout the fake news media."
- Celebrating The Enduring Spirit ($3.1 million): This is a general pro-America ad, with audio of Mr. Trump's July 3 Mount Rushmore speech, extolling the America as the "most successful, most accomplished, most exceptional nation ever to exist in human history."
- To The Great Proud People of Iran ($1.1 million): Footage from the beginning of the Iran War cut together with shots of President Trump as audio from remarks by Mr. Trump and Hegseth play.
- The Country He Loves ($1.4 million) - The "Love Me" ad features Mr. Trump vowing to defeat "communism, socialism and Marxism in America" as a series of flash-cut highlights from his second administration play on the screen. Audio from JMSN's "Love Me" plays throughout the ad, and JMSN has demanded that his song be dropped from the ad.
Asked for comment, the White House referred to an Oct. 5 social media post from Mr. Trump in which he defended the taxpayer-funded ads as "rather standard" but after Republicans criticized the use of taxpayer money to air the ads, he said he would pay for them from his own political fundraising. In a court filing late Saturday, the Justice Department argued that the temporary restraining order was unnecessary because "the alleged offending conduct will end tomorrow."
Legal experts have suggested that the use of taxpayer money for the ads violated a federal statute against congressionally appropriated money being used for "publicity or propaganda" and potentially other laws.
"We are pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda," the plaintiffs said in a statement issued by Democracy Forward, the nonprofit legal organization that represents them. "There is no legal justification — and no precedent — for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda."
In a court declaration Saturday, senior DHS official Holly Mehringer wrote that the money had come from congressionally appropriated funds that are "available for, among other things, 'commemorating efforts and events related to border security.'"
The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements similar to those of past administrations to promote various policies. But the recent ads differ from many past public service announcements because they aren't aimed at helping the public benefit from specific government programs.
A White House official said last month the PSAs "are clearly not political," and noted: "The President is not on the ballot and the ads don't have a call to action."
Top Republicans who criticized the use of public funds include Senate Majority Leader John Thune, of South Dakota. "It shouldn't be paid for with taxpayer dollars," Thune told reporters.
On "Face the Nation," GOP Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana said last month, "I don't think any public official, including President Trump or [former DHS Secretary] Kristi Noem or John Kennedy, should spend public money on private ads for themselves."
The Democratic National Committee has separately sued the Republican administration over the ads.
"This is the sort of government propaganda one might expect in North Korea, not the United States of America, and it is an egregious and illegal misuse of Americans' hard-earned tax dollars," a group of Senate Democrats said in a letter last month.
Amid the backlash, Mr. Trump said he would start paying for the ads with political funds. A White House official said there were no immediate plans to reimburse the government for money already spent.

sources.news_title: US judge orders halt to taxpayer-funded ads featuring Trump
sources.text:
US judge orders halt to taxpayer-funded ads featuring Trump
A US judge on Sunday (Oct 11) blocked the Trump administration from using taxpayer money to pay for political advertisements, after publicly funded television ads glorifying US President Donald Trump began airing in late September and sparked a bipartisan backlash.
Manhattan-based US District Judge Jennifer Rochon temporarily barred the advertisements after plaintiffs including watchdog group Common Cause brought a lawsuit alleging the ads were political propaganda designed to help Republican candidates in the Nov 3 midterm elections, not public service announcements.
The Trump administration was already planning to stop running the ads before Rochon's order, according to a separate statement filed with the court on Saturday.
The decision caps days of controversy over the taxpayer-funded advertisements, which were aired in the final weeks before the midterm elections.
“We won’t stop until this administration is held fully accountable, and no president from any party can waste and abuse taxpayer funds for propaganda ever again," said Common Cause President and CEO Virginia Kase Solomón.
Trump on Monday said he considered the ads to be a "positive promotion for our great USA" but that they would no longer be funded by taxpayers, and the White House said this week that the president's political action committee, MAGA PAC, would fund the ads going forward.
The White House said Trump's political action committee will not reimburse taxpayers for the ads that have already run. The ads end with a disclaimer saying they were paid for by the US government. The Justice Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the judge's order.
The plaintiffs, which also included a public employee union and a candidate for Alabama state representative, had asked Rochon to temporarily block the ads by Friday so that they could not air during weekend programming such as football games and Saturday Night Live.
Democratic Party officials also challenged the ads in a separate suit brought in federal court in Washington.

sources.news_title: Federal judge orders pro-Trump TV ads funded by taxpayers off air immediately
sources.text:
A federal judge ordered the Trump administration on Sunday to stop airing ads funded by the U.S. government that portray President Donald Trump in a favorable light, effective immediately.
The lawsuit was brought by the watchdog group Common Cause; Robert Hunter, a Democratic candidate for a seat in the Alabama state House; and a labor union in New York and its political action committee. The suit was one of several similar complaints — including one by the Democratic National Committee — that were filed to get the ads off the air.
“Plaintiffs have demonstrated that they are likely to succeed on the merits, will suffer irreparable harm in the absence of an injunction, the balance of the equities tips in their favor, and an injunction serves the public interest,” U.S. District Judge Jennifer Rochon of the Southern District of New York wrote.
The administration had said in a court filing Saturday that the Department of Homeland Security, via a vendor, had placed ad buys through Sunday and had told the vendor to not purchase ads beyond that day.
Rochon said the plaintiffs’ argument was not moot, however, and ordered the Trump administration to “cancel or cause to be cancelled” any ads from airing or being disseminated, including those set to air Sunday night.
Rochon also wrote that the administration was barred from using funds appropriated to DHS to “develop, create, disseminate, place, distribute, publish, or air the challenged advertisements.”
The White House, DHS and the Office of Management and Budget, which are all named as defendants in the suit, did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the ruling. MAGA Inc., which Trump had said last week would help him fund the ads moving forward, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
“We are pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda,” the plaintiffs said in a statement. “There is no legal justification — and no precedent — for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda.”
Common Cause President and CEO Virginia Kase Solomón said that despite the ruling, “our fight continues.”
“We won’t stop until this administration is held fully accountable, and no president from any party can waste and abuse taxpayer funds for propaganda ever again,” Solomón said.
The ads — one of which was nearly identical to a 2024 Trump campaign ad — came under scrutiny by critics who argued that using taxpayer money could be illegal and called the spots propaganda.

NEW YORK – A federal judge has ordered President Donald Trump’s administration to halt any remaining television advertisements funded with taxpayer dollars to promote his political agenda. The Sunday night ruling came as administration officials said the $20 million campaign was already nearing its scheduled end.
U.S. District Judge Jennifer L. Rochon in New York granted a request from a coalition that included the nonpartisan watchdog Common Cause, which argued that the advertisements represented an unlawful use of federal funds. Her temporary restraining order directs the government to pull all outstanding ads, including spots scheduled to air Sunday evening.
For the two-week period covered by the order, the administration is barred from entering, renewing or expanding contracts connected to the “development, creation, dissemination, placement, or airing of the challenged advertisements,” Rochon wrote.
The White House did not immediately answer an email seeking comment Sunday night. In a filing submitted late Saturday, the Justice Department maintained that the court order was unnecessary, saying the conduct at issue was expected to end “tomorrow.”
The Department of Homeland Security allocated $20 million in taxpayer funds for the campaign. Legal experts have questioned whether the spending violates a federal law prohibiting the use of congressional appropriations for “publicity or propaganda,” along with potentially other federal statutes. The money came from a broader $175 million package Congress approved for the department as part of Trump’s immigration enforcement strategy.
The White House has characterized the commercials as public service announcements, pointing to similar efforts by previous administrations to explain or promote government policies. Critics argue the Trump ads are different because they do not primarily help people access a specific public program. One commercial also closely mirrors an advertisement Trump used during his 2024 presidential reelection campaign.

sources.news_title: Judge orders Trump administration to immediately stop taxpayer-funded TV ads
sources.text:
A federal judge in New York ordered the Trump administration Sunday night to immediately stop airing controversial government-funded television ads featuring President Donald Trump that critics call political propaganda intended to influence the November midterm election.
The temporary restraining order by Judge Jennifer Rochon in Manhattan federal court also bars the Department of Homeland Security from spending any more of the $20 million allocated for the ad campaign. About $19 million of that allocation has already been spent on the ads.
The order came a day after the Manhattan U.S. Attorney's Office, which is defending the Trump administration in a lawsuit challenging the ads, told Rochon the ads would not continue airing past Sunday.
Rochon's order, which lasts 14 days unless extended, directs the Trump administration to cancel all scheduled ads, including those due to air on Sunday evening. The ads have included the caption "Paid for by the U.S. Government" since they began being aired.
The Manhattan U.S. Attorney's Office declined to comment. The White House didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
Congress appropriated the money for the ads for immigration enforcement.
The coalition of plaintiffs that sued to block the ads told Rochon earlier Sunday that she should issue the TRO despite the U.S. Attorney's Office's claim that the ads would not continue past Sunday.
"Defendants admit that appropriated funds were used to pay for political ads and do not dispute
that this use of taxpayer money is unlawful," the plaintiffs said in a court filing Sunday. 
"Instead, much of Defendants' opposition boils down to a single premise: it is too late for the Court to act. That is not because Defendants have stopped airing the ads," the plaintiffs said. "Indeed, Defendants assert — boldly, given their failure to defend the ads on the merits — that ads will continue to air today, including during evening programming that will attract millions of viewers."
Rochon agreed, saying in her order that the U.S. Attorney's statement that the ads would stop Sunday did not render the TRO request moot. The judge also rejected the Justice Department's argument that the coalition lacked legal standing to challenge the ads.
Rochon said the coalition has shown it is likely to win the lawsuit, would suffer irreparable harm if the TRO is not granted, and that "an injunction serves the public interest."
In addition, the judge ordered the Trump administration not to enter into any new agreements or expand existing ones for the ads. And she stayed a purchase order for the ads between U.S. Customs and Border Protection and a contractor, Lepugh Inc., doing business as LMD Agency Inc.
Rochon said she would soon issue a full opinion explaining her ruling.
The coalition, which filed its lawsuit on Oct. 7, includes the advocacy group Common Cause and the Service Employees International Union Local 32BJ, which is headquartered in New York City.
The Democratic National Committee filed a separate lawsuit challenging the ads that same day.
The ads, which have aired for weeks, drew criticism from Democrats who said they seem designed to help Trump's fellow Republicans in November's election, which will determine which party controls both chambers of Congress.
In its lawsuit, the coalition described one ad, titled "The Country He Loves," as featuring "rapid cuts of photos and videos of President Trump mixed in with text touting what the President views as his accomplishments in office," which includes "Largest Tax Cuts in History;" "Reigniting American Manufacturing;" and "Defend Law and Order and Police."
"Between those messages, the screen repeatedly flashes the words "AMERICA WILL NEVER BE A COMMUNIST COUNTRY," the civil complaint noted.
Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., wrote White House chief of staff Susie Wiles on Sept. 24, a day after that ad first aired.
"The advertisement does not have a clear official government purpose and appears to run afoul of federal prohibitions against the use of appropriated funds as part of 'a general propaganda effort designed to aid a political party or candidates,'" Hassan wrote.
Trump, in response to that criticism, said on Oct. 5 that, going forward, he or his super PAC, MAGA Inc., would pay for the ads. The White House later said the president would not reimburse the federal government for the cost of the ads that had already aired.
In a statement Sunday evening on Rochon's order, the coalition said, "We are pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda."
"There is no legal justification — and no precedent — for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda," the coalition said, referring to Trump.
"As this case moves forward and voters make their voices heard in this election, we will work to ensure the rule of law continues to be upheld, protecting the rights of voters and our democracy."

sources.text:
A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to halt its taxpayer-funded TV ads that closely mirrored campaign rhetoric ahead of the midterms.
Judge Jennifer L. Rochon of the Southern District of New York blocked the administration’s use of the $20 million in taxpayer dollars to “fund the development, creation, and/or airing of the advertisements.”
“Defendants shall cancel or cause to be cancelled any slot, placement, reservation, or arrangement for the airing or dissemination of the challenged advertisements, including those placements for the evening of October 11, 2026,” Rochon, a Biden appointee, wrote in the order.
Rochon’s order barring the ads will remain in effect for two weeks.
Trending
The Department of Homeland Security, which has used its funds to buy airtime, argued in a court filing Saturday that the ads aren’t scheduled beyond Sunday and the administration has not sought any additional media buys. However, Common Cause, a nonpartisan watchdog group that sued the Trump administration over the TV ads, called on Rochon to intervene.
“Beyond their soon-to-be-cessation argument, Defendants offer no guarantee that the ads will not continue beyond today,” Common Cause said in its filing Sunday. “They acknowledge that the contract with the ad agency runs until September 2027.”
Rochon also stayed the contract between the ad firm, LMD Agency, and the Department of Homeland Security. In the Saturday court filing, DHS said that U.S. Customs and Border Protection had issued $20 million to the LMD Agency under a “blanket purchase agreement” but noted the transaction “only funded the airing of preexisting media.”
President Donald Trump has faced public scrutiny and several legal challenges to his administration’s use of up to $20 million in taxpayer funds to run ads ahead of the midterm elections, many of which seem like campaign spots.
Common Cause filed a lawsuit against DHS on Wednesday requesting a temporary restraining order blocking the ads from airing while the legal challenge proceeds. The group also requested an order from the court to bar the government from taking any further action on the ad campaign.
“We are pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda,” Democracy Forward, which is part of the legal team representing the plaintiffs alongside Common Cause, said in a statement. “There is no legal justification — and no precedent — for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda.”
Rochon ordered the decision to be sent to the ad agency immediately, though it was unclear if there was enough time to remove the ads already scheduled
The Trump administration is facing two additional lawsuits from the Democratic National Committee and Democratic Party of Wisconsin concerning the ads. The legal challenges take specific issue with Trump running the ads to promote his agenda, and effectively the Republican Party’s, weeks away from the midterms.
The ads feature stylized edits of the president and other Cabinet officials, with one spot echoing Republican rhetoric on the dangers of communism and another promoting U.S. missile strikes on Iran. Earlier this month, CNN reported at least a dozen ads had been created. Each of the previously aired spots contain a disclaimer reading “Paid for by the U.S. Government.”
In the Saturday court filing, DHS said that U.S. Customs and Border Protection had issued $20 million to the ad firm LMD Agency under a “blanket purchase agreement” but noted the transaction “only funded the airing of preexisting media.”
Holly C. Mehringer, the acting DHS chief financial officer, said in a court affidavit that the department used approximately $19 million for the contract with LMD Agency, leaving potentially around $1 million on the table. Mehringer asserted that DHS will not make any additional media buys past Sunday and any leftover funds “will be de-obligated,” but Common Cause remained unconvinced.
“Considering that Defendants state they will continue to run the ads today, the vague statement that DHS currently has no current ‘plans’ to use the remaining $1,000,000 — which has not been de-obligated and remains available — rings hollow. So too does the limited vow not to use ‘any similar contracts’ to air these ads going forward,” attorneys for the watchdog group wrote.
Congress allocated billions through the “one big, beautiful bill” to DHS for “commemorating efforts and events related to border security.” Initially, the department had only budgeted $1 million for this category, but the White House Office of Management and Budget added the $20 million to the item on Sept. 19. The ads began airing days later on Sept. 23.
The ads have drawn scrutiny from Republican and Democratic lawmakers, who raised questions about whether it is legal to use taxpayer funds for ad campaigns.
In an emailed statement sent to The Washington Sun on Tuesday, the White House characterized the TV-spots as “Presidential Public service announcements” and said they “are nothing new,” citing ad campaigns run by former presidents George W. Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden. Those spots were focused on government-run programs like Obama’s Affordable Care Act.
Trump announced last week on Truth Social that he plans to pay for the ads himself with the help of the money he raised through his super PAC, MAGA Inc — a move that may be illegal under federal campaign finance laws that prohibit a president from directing the spending decisions of a super PAC.
The White House later confirmed that Trump only plans to pay for the ads going forward, and he does not plan to reimburse the government for the millions already spent on the media buys.

sources.news_title: Judge orders Trump to halt taxpayer-funded ads with hours left in administration’s push
sources.text:
(CNN) — A federal judge on Sunday evening ordered the Trump administration to cancel any further airings of the controversial taxpayer-funded ads that promote President Donald Trump’s agenda.
Judge Jennifer Rochon granted a temporary restraining order requested by a coalition led by the nonprofit government watchdog group Common Cause, which had challenged the ad buys in a New York federal court.
The Justice Department told Rochon, an appointee of Joe Biden, late Saturday that the ad push was set to end Sunday night. But Rochon said that timing didn’t render the lawsuit moot and ordered the government to halt any further airings as of 6:45 p.m. ET.
Earlier, the government said in a filing to the court that it has already spent $19 million in taxpayer money on the ads.
The administration allocated $20 million for the ads, which were classified as “public service announcements,” from US Customs and Border Protection, CNN previously reported. An advertising company, LMD Agency Inc., “purchased media buys under the terms of the Order through Sunday, October 11, 2026, at an approximate cost of $19,000,000,” senior Department of Homeland Security official Holly Mehringer said in a sworn declaration in the case.
The Department of Homeland Security, which includes CBP, directed LMD “to not make any additional media buys past October 11,” she added. Mehringer noted there are “no plans” to purchase any additional ads.
Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle expressed concerns about the unprecedented ad campaign when it began late last month.
On October 5, Trump acknowledged the backlash and said “I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.,” his super PAC.
But six days later, the taxpayer-funded ads were still airing.
The Trump administration created at least 13 campaign-style ads, some of which have aired on TV networks including CBS, CNN, MS NOW, Fox News and Fox. Watchdog groups, including the nonprofit, nonpartisan Common Cause, said the ads mark a clear violation of appropriations law restricting the use of federal funding for propaganda or partisan communications. Common Cause and the Democratic National Committee separately sued the Trump administration over the ads.
In a response to the Common Cause lawsuit, the Justice Department said in a filing late Saturday that an effort to halt the spending should be denied because the ads “will not continue past tomorrow.”
The judge’s order Sunday would block any further ad buys for two weeks, so if the administration does consider resuming the ad campaign at taxpayer expense, DOJ lawyers would need to get the court order lifted.
The coalition that brought the suit praised the judge’s order, writing, “We are pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda.”
CNN previously reported that Trump has personally driven the video ads, including helping select the imagery and videos used, according to a source familiar with the matter. Two Trump advisers familiar with the ads said they were being created in-house by the White House video team — which is part of the communications team, responsible for the administration’s public messaging — though at least one of them was produced by a pro-Trump meme group.
Mehringer, in the court filing, described the ads as “depicting the President of the United States and his administration’s various efforts related to protecting America’s borders, including enhancements of border security by combating drug trafficking,” though that is not the exact substance of many of the ads obtained by CNN.
And while the Justice Department conceded the ads “(attack) a generic list of ‘villains,’” it emphasized they did not “address any specific race, electoral candidate, or party.”
A White House spokesperson said Monday that Trump did not plan to reimburse the government for the money already spent on the ad buys, and Mehringer and other officials did not indicate any plans for a refund.
The White House Office of Management and Budget last month allocated $20 million in taxpayer money from CBP for what it called “OBBBA commemorative events.” (OBBBA is an abbreviation for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Trump signed into law in 2025.)
Mehringer emphasized in her declaration that that money “did not fund the creation or production of any videos or media” and “only funded the airing of preexisting media.”
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin was pressed during an appearance Sunday on CBS News’ “Face the Nation” on whether the taxpayer dollars would be refunded.
“Anytime we can do a public service announcement and brag about America, I’m all about it,” Mullin said, taking aim at negative coverage of the Trump administration as he pointed to success in securing the border and lowering fentanyl-related deaths.
“We should be bragging about what’s happening inside America,” he said, adding, “I commend the opportunity of President Trump to give us the opportunity to brag about America.”

Judge orders halt to taxpayer-funded ads featuring Trump
A judge on Sunday blocked the Trump administration from using taxpayer money to pay for political advertisements, after publicly funded television ads glorifying President Donald Trump began airing in late September and sparked a bipartisan backlash.
Manhattan-based U.S. District Judge Jennifer Rochon temporarily barred the advertisements after plaintiffs, including watchdog group Common Cause, brought a lawsuit alleging the ads were political propaganda designed to help Republican candidates in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, not public service announcements.
The Trump administration was already planning to stop running the ads before Rochon’s order, according to a separate statement filed with the court on Saturday.
The decision caps days of controversy over the taxpayer-funded advertisements, which were aired in the final weeks before the midterm elections.
“We won’t stop until this administration is held fully accountable, and no president from any party can waste and abuse taxpayer funds for propaganda ever again,” said Common Cause President and CEO Virginia Kase Solomón.
Trump on Oct. 5 said he considered the ads to be a “positive promotion for our great U.S.A.” but that they would no longer be funded by taxpayers, and the White House said this week that the president’s political action committee, MAGA PAC, would fund the ads going forward.
The White House said Trump’s political action committee will not reimburse taxpayers for the ads that have already run. The ads end with a disclaimer saying they were paid for by the U.S. government. The Justice Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the judge’s order.
The plaintiffs, which also included a public employee union and a candidate for Alabama state representative, had asked Rochon to temporarily block the ads by Friday so that they could not air during weekend programming such as football games and Saturday Night Live.
Democratic Party officials also challenged the ads in a separate suit brought in federal court in Washington.
